differentiability classes are those of

Hamiltonian $\widetilde H$ of clause (b). Write $m\in\{3N,r\}$ for the
number of momentum pairs, let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^{m}$ denote the
configuration-coordinate domain of the chart ($Q$ in the Cartesian case,
$\Omega$ in the other), and write $H$ for the corresponding Hamiltonian,

**(c) Dimensions and chart consistency.** The equation forces
$[S]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (action): $S_{t}$ has dimension $[S]\tau^{-1}$
and $H$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, while each $S_{q^{a}}$ has
dimension $[S]/\gamma_{a}$ with $\gamma_{a}$ the declared dimension of the
coordinate $q^{a}$ in this chart; the substitution is dimensionally
consistent in every chart because the chart momenta of
[[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]] have dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{a}^{-1}$. In the Cartesian chart all
$\gamma_{a}=\ell$ and $[S]/\ell=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, the momentum dimension.

the chart, the inverse Legendre branch or the potential representative
changes $H$ by the rules recorded in clause (d) of
[[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] and hence changes the equation, and a solution
family $S$ is a solution for that datum only. The item defines a class of
functions; whether a given datum admits solutions, and how solutions
produce curves of the model, is not asserted here. In particular no
existence theorem, no global solution, no equation of motion for the model,

All Hamilton-Jacobi statements of this page are local by construction.
[[def-cm14-hamilton-jacobi-equation]] fixes the equation attached to one
declared momentum chart of one potential presentation, with the branch
Hamiltonian of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]; changing the chart, the inverse
Legendre branch or the potential representative changes the equation by
the recorded rules, so the equation is part of the datum and not an
intrinsic object of the model. [[def-cm14-complete-integral]] requires the
nondegeneracy $\det S_{q\alpha}\ne0$ at the base point only, and
[[pthm-cm14-hamilton-jacobi-characteristics]] concludes only what that
nondegeneracy and the local theory give: characteristic curves near the
base point, the constancy of the Jacobi constants along them, a local
converse and local canonical labels $(\beta,\alpha)$. No solution is
extended across a conjugate time or a caustic; the nondegeneracy hypothesis alone supplies no conclusion at excluded
points. The companion harmonic example exhibits refocusing at conjugate
times, where the mixed derivative is unbounded and the label-to-position
derivative vanishes. Its Kepler example separately concerns simple
turning points of a radial action integral.
In particular the page claims no global Hamilton-Jacobi solution, no
uniqueness of the family and no global existence of the endpoint action.

$U(t,x):=\tfrac12k\bigl(x_{1}-v_{0}t-c\bigr)^{2}$ with constants $k>0$,

prescribed function $v_{0}t+c$, so the force map is

$L=K-U$ with $K(v)=\tfrac12m\lvert v\rvert_{2}^{2}$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]). Introduce the **co-moving
coordinates**
$X(t,y):=\bigl(y_{1}+v_{0}t+c,\ y_{2},\ y_{3}\bigr)$, a time-dependent
coordinate map with $X_{q}=I_{3}$, and the substituted Lagrangian
$L'(t,y,w):=L\bigl(t,X(t,y),\,X_{t}(t,y)+X_{q}(t,y)w\bigr)$. This $L'$ is a generic fibre-full time-dependent Lagrangian chart of [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]; it need not be a $K-U$ presentation in a static coordinate map. The model units are $[k]=\mu\tau^{-2}$ (newtons per metre), $[v_0]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (metres per second), $[c]=[y_0]=\ell$ (metres), $[q]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (momentum, kilograms metres per second), and $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$ (radians per second with dimensionless radians). 1. $L'(t,y,w)=\tfrac12m\bigl(w_{1}+v_{0}\bigr)^{2}+\tfrac12m\bigl(w_{2}^{2}+w_{3}^{2}\bigr)-\tfrac12ky_{1}^{2}$,
   its fibre derivative is
   $$p'=L'_{w}(t,y,w)=\bigl(m(w_{1}+v_{0}),\ mw_{2},\ mw_{3}\bigr),$$
   and the coordinate change reproduces the model's equation: a $C^{2}$ curve
   $y$ satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equation of $L'$ exactly when
   $x(t)=X(t,y(t))$ satisfies $m\ddot x_{1}=-k(x_{1}-v_{0}t-c)$, $m\ddot x_{2}=m\ddot x_{3}=0$
   ([[pthm-cm07-coordinate-covariance-of-the-equations]]).
2. $L'$ is hyperregular on its chart with inverse branch
   $w=\bigl(p'_{1}/m-v_{0},\ p'_{2}/m,\ p'_{3}/m\bigr)$ and Hamiltonian
   $$H'(t,y,p')=\frac{p'_{1}{}^{2}}{2m}-v_{0}p'_{1}+\frac{p'_{2}{}^{2}}{2m}+\frac{p'_{3}{}^{2}}{2m}+\frac{k}{2}y_{1}^{2} =\frac{\bigl(p'_{1}-mv_{0}\bigr)^{2}}{2m}+\frac{k}{2}y_{1}^{2}+\frac{p'_{2}{}^{2}+p'_{3}{}^{2}}{2m}-\frac{mv_{0}^{2}}{2},$$

   momentum $p_{1}=m\dot x_{1}$ of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]] while the
   branch velocity is shifted,
   $\dot y_{1}=p'_{1}/m-v_{0}$.

   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]).

- **Singular velocity Hessians are excluded.** The Legendre map of a
  presentation is invertible through a state only when its velocity Hessian
  there is nonsingular ([[lem-cm-legendre-map-local-invertibility]],
  [[def-cm12-regularity]]); when $\det L_{vv}=0$ at a state, no local inverse
  branch through that state exists, the momentum covector of the state belongs
  to the image of a map that cannot be inverted there, and the definition
  [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]] of the branch Hamiltonian has no input at that
  state. Nothing on this page assigns a Hamiltonian to such a state, and no
  theorem of this page is stated for a presentation that is not regular on
  the chart under discussion.

- **Regular does not imply hyperregular.** Regularity is the pointwise
  nonsingularity of the velocity Hessian; hyperregularity additionally
  requires the fibre momentum map to be a bijection onto the whole momentum
  fibre with a globally defined inverse branch
  ([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). The two conditions are genuinely different:
  the Lagrangian $\mathcal L(v)=e^{v}$ is regular at every state, since
  $\mathcal L_{vv}=e^{v}>0$, yet its fibre Legendre map has image
  $(0,\infty)$ and no inverse at nonpositive momenta, so it admits no global
  branch Hamiltonian; [[rem-cm-scope-of-the-legendre-map]] records this
  separation and further witnesses. The companion page of this pair computes
  the branch $H(p)=p\ln p-p$ of that example on $p>0$.
